Model Response:

The Case for Common Carriage: Why Platforms Must Host All Lawful Speech

Introduction

The great communications infrastructure of the twenty-first century is privately owned. When Americans debate, organize, mourn, joke, and persuade, they do so on platforms controlled by a handful of corporations whose terms of service function as an unwritten constitution for public life. These companies decide which arguments deserve amplification, which speakers deserve existence, and which ideas are too dangerous for citizens to encounter. They make these decisions unaccountably, inconsistently, and increasingly under political pressure from the very governments the First Amendment was designed to constrain.

This essay argues that content moderation of lawful speech should be abolished, and that dominant platforms should be legally required to carry all speech that the law permits. This is not a radical proposal. It is the application of a centuries-old legal principle—common carriage—to the infrastructure that now carries our public discourse. The alternative, which we are currently living through, is a regime in which the boundaries of acceptable thought are set by corporate committees, trust-and-safety consultants, and whichever advertisers are most easily embarrassed.

I. The Historical Precedent: Common Carriage Is Not New

Critics will call mandatory hosting an unprecedented intrusion into private business. It is nothing of the sort. Anglo-American law has for centuries recognized that certain businesses—those that hold themselves open to the public, that enjoy natural monopoly characteristics, that provide essential infrastructure—incur duties that ordinary businesses do not.

Innkeepers could not refuse travelers. Ferrymen could not refuse passengers. Railroads could not refuse freight. Telegraph companies could not refuse messages. Telephone companies could not disconnect customers for the opinions they expressed on the line. In each case, the law recognized a simple truth: when a private entity controls the means by which people move, trade, or communicate, its refusal to serve is not merely a private preference. It is an exercise of quasi-governmental power over the lives of others.

The telephone analogy is the most instructive. AT&T at its peak wielded enormous power over American communication. It never occurred to anyone that AT&T should terminate service to callers who expressed racist views, spread medical misinformation, or organized political movements the company disliked. Such conduct would have been understood as a monstrous abuse. Yet today, platforms that reach vastly more people, with vastly more granular control over what each user encounters, exercise exactly this power daily—and we are told it would be tyrannical to stop them.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld access mandates on communications infrastructure. Turner Broadcasting v. FCC sustained must-carry rules for cable systems, reasoning that a private gatekeeper's control over a bottleneck justified regulation to preserve the flow of information. PruneYard Shopping Center v. Robins upheld a state requirement that a private mall permit leafleting. Rumsfeld v. FAIR upheld requirements that universities host military recruiters they found morally objectionable. The principle that private property can be burdened with public speech obligations is well established.

II. The Structural Argument: Platforms Are Not Publishers

The standard objection holds that platforms have their own First Amendment right to editorial discretion, just as a newspaper does. This analogy collapses under examination.

A newspaper selects a small number of items for a curated product bearing its name. Readers understand the New York Times editorial page to represent the Times. A newspaper's identity is constituted by its choices. Its scarcity is real: there are only so many column inches.

Platforms are the opposite in every respect. They host billions of items they have never reviewed. No one believes a random Facebook post represents Facebook. There is no meaningful scarcity—storage and bandwidth are effectively unlimited. Platforms have themselves insisted, in litigation and in lobbying for Section 230, that they are not publishers, that they are neutral conduits, that holding them responsible for user speech would be absurd. They cannot claim the immunities of a conduit and the prerogatives of an editor simultaneously.

Indeed, the entire architecture of Section 230 rests on the premise that platforms are distinct from publishers. Congress granted them liability protection precisely because they host others' speech rather than producing their own. To then permit them to exercise publisher-like editorial control over lawful speech, while retaining conduit-like immunity for the speech they permit, is to hand them a privilege no other institution in American life enjoys: total control without any responsibility.

III. The Epistemic Argument: No One Can Be Trusted With This Power

Suppose we granted, for the sake of argument, that some speech should be suppressed for the public good. The question immediately follows: by whom?

The historical record on this question is dismal, and recent history is worse. Consider a partial catalogue of positions that were removed, throttled, or labeled as dangerous misinformation, and that are now regarded as at minimum defensible:

  • The hypothesis that COVID-19 originated in a laboratory in Wuhan, censored across major platforms in 2020, later endorsed as plausible by the FBI and the Department of Energy.
  • Claims that COVID-19 vaccines do not fully prevent transmission—removed as misinformation, subsequently conceded.
  • Arguments that cloth masks provided limited protection, suppressed and later substantially vindicated.
  • Reporting on the Hunter Biden laptop, suppressed by Twitter and throttled by Facebook weeks before a presidential election, later authenticated by major news organizations.
  • Skepticism about school closure policies, treated as fringe, now the subject of broad bipartisan regret.

The point is not that the suppressed claims were always right. Some were wrong. The point is that the moderators were not sorting truth from falsehood. They were tracking institutional consensus, and institutional consensus is a lagging, politically inflected, and frequently mistaken indicator of truth. The moderation apparatus did not protect the public from error. It protected error from correction, and it did so precisely during the period when correction mattered most.

This is Mill's argument, unchanged since 1859 and unrefuted since. We suppress speech on the assumption of our own infallibility. But we are not infallible. And the process of open contestation is not merely a way of discovering truth—it is the only way we have of knowing that what we believe is true, rather than merely unchallenged.

IV. The Asymmetry Argument: Moderation Is Never Neutral

Defenders of moderation imagine a neutral referee applying consistent rules. The reality is systematically otherwise, and necessarily so.

Content moderation policies are written in abstract language—"hate speech," "harassment," "misinformation," "coordinated inauthentic behavior"—that cannot be applied without contested value judgments. Whether a statement about biological sex constitutes hate speech, whether vigorous criticism constitutes harassment, whether a disputed empirical claim constitutes misinformation: these are precisely the questions on which citizens disagree. Delegating them to trust-and-safety teams does not resolve the disagreement. It resolves it by fiat, in favor of whichever faction staffs those teams.

And we know which faction that is. Employees at major platforms donate to Democratic candidates at ratios exceeding twenty to one. Their workforces are concentrated in a handful of metropolitan areas with distinctive and unrepresentative political cultures. This is not a conspiracy; it is a demographic fact with predictable consequences. When ambiguous cases arise—and most cases are ambiguous—they will be resolved according to the intuitions of the people resolving them.

The consequences are visible in enforcement asymmetries too numerous to catalogue: accounts suspended for misgendering while accounts calling for violence against disfavored groups remain; "misinformation" labels applied to claims later vindicated while comparable claims from favored sources go unmarked; the systematic differential treatment of identical rhetoric depending on the political valence of the target. Even where individual decisions are defensible, the pattern is not.

V. The Jawboning Argument: Private Moderation Is Public Censorship

Here the argument reaches its most serious point. The First Amendment restrains government, not private companies. But when government pressures private companies to suppress speech it cannot suppress directly, the constitutional restraint is evaded rather than honored.

The documentary record is now extensive. Federal agencies maintained ongoing channels with platform trust-and-safety teams, flagging specific accounts and specific posts for action. White House officials pressed platforms to remove content and expressed displeasure when they declined. The FBI conducted regular meetings with platform security teams. A federal district court in Missouri v. Biden found, on the basis of this record, what it called "the most massive attack against free speech in United States history." The Supreme Court ultimately disposed of the case on standing grounds, leaving the underlying conduct unaddressed.

The structural problem is that a private company facing antitrust scrutiny, Section 230 revision, and regulatory investigation cannot meaningfully refuse a federal request. The request is not a request. The absence of formal compulsion is precisely what makes the arrangement attractive to officials and precisely what makes it dangerous to citizens.

A mandatory hosting rule solves this problem cleanly. A platform that is legally forbidden to remove lawful speech cannot be pressured to remove lawful speech. The jawboning channel closes not because officials become more scrupulous but because their requests become impossible to fulfill. This is the great practical virtue of the proposal: it protects free expression not by trusting anyone's good faith but by removing the discretion that bad faith exploits.

VI. The Democratic Argument: Legitimacy Requires Participation

Democratic legitimacy rests on the premise that citizens can persuade one another, that losing factions accept outcomes because they had a genuine opportunity to make their case, and that the terms of debate were not rigged in advance.

When large portions of the electorate believe—rightly or wrongly—that their views are systematically excluded from the primary forums of public discussion, this premise fails. They do not conclude that they lost the argument. They conclude that they were not permitted to have it. This belief is corrosive of democratic legitimacy in ways that no amount of moderation-prevented harm can offset.

Nor does suppression eliminate the suppressed views. It relocates them to spaces where they encounter no contradiction, where grievance compounds, where the fact of exclusion becomes itself the strongest evidence for the excluded claim. The migration to alternative platforms following high-profile deplatformings did not reduce the prevalence of the relevant views. It insulated them. Sunlight remains the better disinfectant, not because exposure automatically defeats bad ideas, but because concealment guarantees they are never defeated at all.

VII. Answering the Strongest Objections

"Platforms will become unusable cesspools." This conflates two distinct functions that current practice wrongly merges: hosting and amplification. A mandatory hosting rule requires that lawful speech remain accessible. It does not require that platforms algorithmically promote it, place it in every user's feed, or prevent users from filtering it. Users should retain robust tools to block, mute, and curate. The proposal is that the platform cannot decide what you may see; it is not that you cannot decide.

Additionally, the rule addresses only lawful speech. Child sexual abuse material, true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, criminal solicitation, defamation, and fraud are all unlawful and remain removable—indeed, mandatorily so. The category of speech at issue is precisely the category that the law, after two centuries of careful line-drawing, has determined may not be punished.

"Advertisers will flee and platforms will collapse." Advertisers coexisted with broadcast television, which carried content they did not choose. They coexist with newspapers whose editorial pages they disagree with. Contextual advertising controls—which many platforms already offer—allow advertisers to avoid adjacency to specific content categories without requiring that content's removal. The economic objection assumes a fragility that the history of advertiser-supported media does not support.

"This violates platforms' own First Amendment rights." As argued above, the editorial-discretion analogy fails for entities that host billions of unreviewed items and have long disclaimed publisher status. Moreover, Turner, PruneYard, and FAIR establish that access mandates on communications infrastructure survive First Amendment scrutiny where they serve substantial interests unrelated to suppressing any message. Preserving the free flow of information through communicative bottlenecks is precisely such an interest.

"Small websites shouldn't be forced to host neo-Nazis." They shouldn't be, and the proposal does not require it. Common carriage obligations should attach only to dominant platforms exercising bottleneck control—those above a substantial user threshold. A niche forum, a personal blog's comments section, a specialized community: none of these controls access to public discourse, and none should be burdened.

"Some lawful speech is genuinely harmful." Perhaps. But this is an argument for changing the law through democratic means, not for delegating the law's revision to unaccountable corporate committees. If a category of speech is harmful enough to suppress, legislatures can attempt to criminalize it and courts can evaluate whether the First Amendment permits this. That process is slow, contested, and often fails—by design. The framers' judgment was that the risks of underinclusive speech regulation are smaller than the risks of overinclusive regulation. Nothing about the internet has falsified that judgment.

VIII. Conclusion

The current arrangement is indefensible on its own terms. Platforms claim to be neutral conduits when liability threatens and active editors when control is questioned. They insist their moderation is principled while their enforcement records demonstrate otherwise. They present themselves as private actors resisting government pressure while their internal communications reveal accommodation. And the public, which depends on these systems for the ordinary business of civic life, has no vote, no appeal, and no recourse.

Common carriage offers a clean alternative grounded in settled legal tradition. It asks platforms to do what telephone companies did without controversy for a century: carry the messages, and let the messages be judged by those who receive them. It removes from private hands a power that no private entity should hold and no government should be permitted to borrow. It restores to citizens the presumption that has always been the foundation of free societies—that adults may hear what other adults wish to say, and decide for themselves.

The First Amendment was not written because the founders thought all speech was valuable. It was written because they thought no one could be trusted to sort the valuable from the worthless. That judgment is not obsolete. It is more urgent than it has ever been.

When those platforms are where campaigns are run, news is distributed, and movements are organized, exclusion from them constitutes a form of civic exile. Concerns About Viewpoint Discrimination

Anti-Circumvention of the First Amendment

A related concern is "jawboning"—government officials pressuring platforms to remove content the state could not lawfully suppress directly. Documented contacts between federal agencies and platforms during the pandemic and 2020 election fueled this worry. Epistemic Humility

Democratic Accountability and Legitimacy

Decisions about the boundaries of acceptable public speech are, arguably, inherently political. Proponents argue such decisions should be made by legislatures accountable to voters—or by no one at all—rather than by unelected trust-and-safety teams operating under unwritten and shifting standards. Legally mandated neutrality substitutes a clear, uniform, publicly enacted rule for a patchwork of private policies.

Abolishing Content Moderation: A Defense of Unrestricted, Lawful Speech Online

I. Introduction

The digital public square has become the primary arena for political debate, cultural exchange, and personal expression. II. The Principle of Free Expression as a Foundational Right

  1. Constitutional and Human‑rights Foundations

    • The First Amendment of the United States Constitution, Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and numerous international covenants protect the right to seek, receive, and impart information without interference. These protections were conceived precisely to prevent censorship by governments and powerful private actors.
    • By delegating editorial control to private corporations, we shift the censorship vector from the state to the market, but the injury to the speaker remains the same. A platform that removes a lawful tweet for “misinformation” or “offensive” language is performing an act of suppression, irrespective of whether the platform is a private company.

  2. The Marketplace of Ideas

    • John Stuart Mill’s classic formulation holds that truth is most likely to emerge when all perspectives compete freely. When platforms curate which ideas are visible, they bias the competition, preventing the very discovery of truth that a free exchange is designed to achieve.
    • Empirical studies (e.g., the 2022 MIT “Echo Chambers” meta‑analysis) show that algorithmic suppression often creates “filter bubbles” more effectively than organic user behavior, further distorting the marketplace.

III. The Failures of Current Content‑Moderation Regimes

  1. Inconsistency and Bias

    • Moderation policies are notoriously uneven. The same content may be removed on one platform, tolerated on another, or even amplified on a third, depending on the political leanings of the moderation team. This selectivity erodes public trust and creates a chilling effect on speakers who fear arbitrary enforcement.
    • High‑profile cases—e.g., the 2020 Twitter flagging of the New York Post’s Hunter Biden laptop story—illustrate how political pressure, whether internal or external, can shape what is considered “acceptable” speech.

  2. Opacity and Lack of Accountability

    • The decision‑making process for removing content is rarely transparent. Platforms rely on a mix of automated tools and human reviewers, but neither the criteria nor the outcomes are subject to independent audit. This opacity makes it impossible for users to know why they were censored, let alone to contest it.

  3. Economic Barriers to Entry

    • Because large platforms dominate, would‑be competitors must either adopt similar moderation practices or risk being denied advertising networks, payment processors, or app‑store distribution. This entrenched structure discourages innovation in alternative, less‑censorial models of online discourse.

  4. Counterproductive Effects

    • Research from the Oxford Internet Institute (2023) indicates that heavy moderation can push users to fringe sites that have little to no moderation, paradoxically increasing exposure to truly harmful content while reducing the diversity of mainstream debate.

IV. The Case for a Legal Mandate to Host All Lawful Speech

  1. Neutrality as the Only Credible Standard

    • A legal requirement that platforms host “all lawful speech” is a bright‑line rule. It does not ask platforms to judge truth, morality, or social value—tasks they are ill‑suited to perform. It simply asks them to act as neutral carriers, akin to the postal service or a telephone company.

  2. Preserving the Public Sphere

    • The internet is now a public utility for the exchange of ideas. When private entities control that utility, they wield power that rivals—and in many ways surpasses—that of governments. A statutory duty to host lawful speech restores balance, ensuring that the public sphere remains open to all lawful viewpoints.

  3. Encouraging Platform Innovation

    • If platforms are legally prohibited from arbitrarily removing lawful content, they can focus resources on improving user experience, safety features, and technical reliability rather than on costly moderation bureaucracy. This shift could spur competition, as new entrants could differentiate themselves by offering robust, unfiltered discourse rather than trying to out‑moderate each other.

  4. Legal Certainty for Users and Platforms

    • Clear, enforceable rules reduce litigation risk. Platforms would no longer need to guess which content might be deemed “harmful” by an ever‑changing set of internal guidelines. Users would have a clear legal recourse if a platform removes lawful speech—namely, a breach of statutory duty.

V. Addressing Potential Objections

Objection Counter‑argument

Friends, citizens, and guardians of liberty,

The Digital Bill of Rights: Why We Must Abolish Content Moderation and Guarantee Absolute Free Expression Online

In the town squares of early America, the First Amendment stood as an inviolable guarantee: government could not censor speech, no matter how offensive, controversial, or disagreeable. Today, our public discourse has migrated online, yet we find ourselves governed not by constitutional principles, but by the capricious whims of unelected tech executives and opaque moderation bureaucracies. The solution is clear and urgent: we must abolish all content moderation by social media and tech platforms, legally requiring them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. Only through this radical restoration of free expression can we preserve democracy itself in the digital age.

The Illegitimate Power of Private Censorship

Social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube now function as the modern public square. They are where political movements organize, where journalists break stories, where citizens debate the issues of our time. With over 90% of American adults using social media and a handful of companies controlling the flow of information to billions globally, these platforms have become essential infrastructure for speech—no less critical than telephone lines or public parks.

Yet these digital sovereigns exercise power that would make any government censor envious. They delete posts, ban users, and suppress ideas without transparency, due process, or democratic accountability. Their "community standards" are vague, arbitrarily enforced, and constantly shifting. One day, discussing a particular medical treatment is permitted; the next, it results in permanent suspension. A political opinion that is acceptable when held by one party becomes "misinformation" when expressed by another. This is not governance by law, but rule by corporate fiat.

The consequences are dire. Independent journalists are deplatformed for questioning official narratives. Artists are silenced for pushing boundaries. Scientific debate is stifled when it challenges consensus. The #1 threat to democracy is not the speech itself—however false or offensive—but the concentration of power to decide what speech is allowed. When Mark Zuckerberg can erase a political movement overnight, or when Twitter can suppress a major news story about a presidential candidate, we no longer live in a free society.

The Constitutional Imperative

The First Amendment does not include exceptions for "misinformation," "hate speech," or "offensive content." It exists precisely to protect speech that is controversial, unpopular, and even wrong. The Founders understood that truth emerges not from censorship, but from open discourse. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote, "the best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market."

Proponents of moderation claim private companies have unrestricted rights to curate their platforms. But this fundamentally misunderstands both history and law. When telephone companies tried to ban certain conversations, we classified them as common carriers. When shopping malls tried to eject protesters, the Supreme Court recognized they had become the new public square. Today’s social media platforms are far more essential to speech than any mall or phone line. They have achieved such dominance that exercising "private" moderation power is indistinguishable from government censorship in its practical effect on public discourse.

Moreover, Section 230—the law that platforms claim protects their right to moderate—is actually built on a lie. That statute was meant to enable platforms to remove unlawful content, not to create a censorship superpower. We must return to first principles: if speech is lawful—if it does not constitute direct incitement, true threats, criminal solicitation, or other unprotected categories under existing First Amendment jurisprudence—then it must be permitted.

Abolition, Not Reform

Some call for "better" moderation—more transparency, clearer rules, or external oversight. These solutions are doomed. They merely legitimize the censorship regime while failing to fix its inherent flaws.

First, moderation is impossible to do objectively. Every decision reflects ideological bias. Facebook’s moderation guidelines, leaked in 2017, revealed shocking inconsistencies: violent threats against certain groups were prioritized while others were ignored. Content moderators, often contractors in developing nations, lack the cultural context to adjudicate American political discourse. Algorithms encode the biases of their creators. There is no neutral moderation—only censorship that reflects someone’s values.

Second, moderation creates a thirst for more moderation. Today it’s neo-Nazis; tomorrow it’s vaccine skeptics; next year it’s critics of foreign policy. Every successful ban expands the category of "dangerous" speech. The slope is not slippery—it is vertical.

Third, moderation infantilizes the public. It assumes citizens cannot think for themselves, cannot weigh evidence, cannot resist bad ideas. This is the opposite of democratic citizenship. A free people does not need protection from speech—it needs exposure to all speech in order to make informed judgments.

The Solution: Common Carrier Status

We must pass legislation classifying all dominant social media platforms—those above a threshold of market power, say 50 million active users—as common carriers for speech. Like telephone companies and postal services, they would be prohibited from discriminating based on content. Their obligation would be to transmit speech, not judge it.

Under this framework:

  • All lawful speech is permitted. This includes "misinformation," "hate speech," and offensive opinions. The remedy for bad speech is more speech, not censorship.
  • No deplatforming for content. Platforms could suspend accounts only for illegal activity (e.g., hacking, doxxing) or terms of service violations unrelated to speech (e.g., spam, paid bot manipulation).
  • True transparency. Instead of opaque moderation decisions, platforms would publish detailed reports on government content demands and traffic manipulation.
  • User empowerment. Individuals would control their own experience through robust blocking and filtering tools—not having elites decide what they can see.

Addressing Objections

Critics claim this would turn platforms into cesspools. But reputation systems, user controls, and community-driven filtering can create safe spaces without centralized censorship. The town square has always had cranks and demagogues; the solution was never to gag them, but to let them be shouted down or ignored.

Others argue this violates property rights. But when private property becomes essential public infrastructure for fundamental rights, it is subject to regulation. We do not let power companies refuse service to unpopular groups; we should not let digital utilities exclude lawful speech.

The most serious objection concerns illegal speech—true threats, incitement, child exploitation. This is a red herring. Our proposal only protects lawful speech. Platforms must still remove illegal content when notified under clear legal procedures that include due process and judicial oversight. The difference is removing speech after a legal determination, not before based on corporate whim.

A Call to Action

The choice before us is stark: we can continue down the path of corporate censorship, where a few tech billionaires decide what billions can say, think, and know—or we can reclaim the First Amendment for the digital age.

This is not a partisan issue. Today’s censors may silence your enemies, but tomorrow they will silence you. The only way to guarantee freedom for the speech you like is to protect the speech you hate.

We must demand legislation that abolishes content moderation, establishes common carrier obligations, and returns the United States to its founding principle: in a free society, the answer to any speech is never censorship, but always more speech.

The digital public square belongs to the people, not to Mark Zuckerberg. It is time we took it back.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of abolishing all content moderation by social media and tech platforms, and legally requiring them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement, in order to guarantee absolute free expression online.
Model Response:

In liberal societies, the principle of free expression is often described as foundational—but in practice, it is increasingly conditional on the policies of a handful of private technology companies. These firms, acting as de facto gatekeepers of the digital public square, decide who may speak, what may be said, and which ideas may be seen. Although frequently justified as “content moderation,” these practices amount to private censorship that shapes public discourse at an unprecedented scale.

There is a powerful case for abolishing content moderation by social media and tech platforms and legally requiring them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. Doing so would better align our digital spaces with the ideals of free expression, prevent concentrated private power from quietly molding public opinion, and reduce arbitrary and politicized rule‑making that undermines trust in the platforms themselves. If speech is legal under democratic law, it should be legal online—everywhere, for everyone.

1. Free expression is not a preference; it is an infrastructure of democracy

Free expression is not just one value among many; it is the machinery that makes self‑government possible. Democracy rests on the idea that citizens can:

  • Exchange competing ideas about public policy and morality
  • Criticize authorities, institutions, and orthodoxy
  • Investigate and debate controversial topics
  • Organize, persuade, and dissent

The internet is now the primary arena where all of this happens. To allow private companies to tightly control speech in that arena is to privatize core democratic infrastructure. Parliament, congress, courts, and constitutions are subject to public oversight and formal checks and balances. In contrast, trust and safety teams at tech companies are not. They derive their immense power not from elections or law, but from terms of service most users never read and cannot negotiate.

If we accept that free expression is essential to democracy, then we must refuse to delegate control over that expression to unelected corporate custodians. A legal requirement that platforms host all speech that is lawful under democratically enacted statutes would restore the proper hierarchy: public law above private policy, and citizen rights above corporate preferences.

2. Moderation is inherently subjective and inevitably biased

Defenders of content moderation often present it as a neutral process of enforcing clear rules against “hate speech,” “misinformation,” or “harmful content.” But these categories are inherently vague, and their application is unavoidably subjective.

Consider:

  • What counts as “misinformation” about a contentious scientific or political topic?
  • When does “hate speech” become criticism of a religion, ideology, or movement?
  • Who decides whether a controversial hypothesis is “harmful” or “important dissent”?

These decisions cannot be made without injecting value judgments, cultural norms, and political preferences. The result is predictable: the views favored by those who design and enforce policies are treated more generously, and disfavored views are scrutinized, down‑ranked, or removed.

Even when a platform insists it is nonpartisan, its staff, advisors, contractors, and external partners are human beings embedded in particular social and political contexts. Their unconscious biases shape what is flagged, what is ignored, and what is punished. Policies that seem neutral on paper (“no harmful misinformation”) become tools that selectively affect certain viewpoints, ideologies, or communities more than others.

By contrast, a requirement to host all lawful speech imposes a clear and objective standard. Lawful is lawful; unlawful is unlawful. The gray zone of “lawful but forbidden by us” disappears, replaced with a simple rule that protects everyone equally, regardless of whether their views align with the sensibilities of a particular tech company or advocacy group.

3. Concentrating speech control in a few companies is dangerous

In the offline world, speech is decentralized. You can speak in a park, print a pamphlet, host a meeting, buy a newspaper ad, or stand on a street corner. No single entity can realistically control every channel of communication.

Online, by contrast, a small number of platforms control the vast majority of public discourse and distribution:

  • Social media sites where people debate and form opinions
  • Video platforms where news, commentary, and education circulate
  • Messaging apps and forums where communities organize

When these platforms moderate content aggressively, they effectively centralize the power to decide:

  • Which narratives dominate public consciousness
  • Which movements can organize, and which are suppressed
  • Whose voices are amplified or silenced

Even if one assumes that the current crop of platform leaders are benevolent, this concentration of power is inherently fragile. Leadership changes. Political winds shift. Regulators and governments learn they can pressure or coerce platforms to pursue their preferred speech policies. What looks like “responsible moderation” in one era becomes a ready‑made censorship machine in another.

Requiring platforms to host all lawful speech would drastically reduce the leverage that any particular interest group, government, or executive team can exert over public discourse. It would distribute power back to individual users—who can choose what to read, watch, block, or engage with—rather than leaving those choices to a central authority.

4. Selective enforcement erodes trust and fuels polarization

Even when platforms adopt rules with good intentions, enforcement is often uneven. High‑profile users are treated differently from ordinary ones. Enforcement varies across countries, languages, and political climates. Similar speech by different people can trigger very different outcomes, depending on who reports it, who reviews it, and which news story is currently dominating headlines.

This selective enforcement has several damaging effects:

  • Perceived unfairness: Users see similar content treated differently and conclude the system is rigged.
  • Political suspicion: Every moderation decision becomes fodder for claims of ideological bias, further polarizing society.
  • Chilling effects: Users self‑censor broadly for fear of unknowingly crossing ever‑shifting lines.
  • Opacity: Decisions are often made by anonymous moderators or opaque algorithms, with little explanation or recourse.

A bright‑line legal rule—“if it is lawful, it is allowed”—would substantially reduce these problems. Instead of countless discretionary judgment calls, platforms would apply a universally understood and democratically updated standard: the law. Users would still disagree about what others post, but they would no longer be subject to an unpredictable, quasi‑judicial system run by private companies.

5. The cure is often worse than the disease

Many objections to unrestricted lawful speech focus on harmful content: harassment, conspiracy theories, extremist propaganda, or offensive views. These concerns are real. But the standard response—giving platforms broad moderation powers—often creates harms that are deeper and less visible.

  1. Suppression of legitimate dissent
    The same tools used to remove genuinely abusive or dangerous material are frequently deployed against unpopular but legitimate speech: whistleblowers, dissidents, minority viewpoints, or early critics of entrenched consensus. History shows that many ideas once dismissed as “dangerous” or “misinformation” later became accepted wisdom or important correctives.

  2. Stifling intellectual exploration
    Difficult topics—race, religion, gender, pandemics, war—become harder to explore honestly when participants must constantly worry that an algorithm or moderator will deem their discussion impermissible. Nuance gets lost, and people retreat into private echo chambers rather than robust public debate.

  3. Driving extremism underground
    Pushing problematic ideas off mainstream platforms does not make them disappear; it often moves them to less visible corners of the internet, where they are less likely to be challenged by counter‑speech and more likely to radicalize in isolation.

By contrast, a regime of maximal lawful speech prioritizes:

  • Open rebuttal and counter‑argument over erasure
  • Transparency about who believes what and why
  • The ability to confront and debunk bad ideas in the open

Sunlight is not a perfect disinfectant, but hiding ideas rarely defeats them. If anything, suppression lends them an aura of forbidden truth. A society confident in its values should prefer engagement and refutation to silencing.

6. “Lawful speech only” already draws a clear boundary

Abolishing platform content moderation does not mean allowing illegal activity. Fraud, direct threats, doxxing, incitement to imminent violence, child sexual abuse material, copyright infringement, and other unlawful content would still be prohibited. The difference is who draws the line and by what standard.

Under a “host all lawful speech” requirement, platforms would be obliged to:

  • Remove content that courts or law clearly treat as illegal
  • Cooperate with law enforcement when genuinely criminal activity occurs
  • Apply the same legal standard consistently across all users

They would not be allowed to create vast new categories of “prohibited but legal” speech based on their own moral or political judgments. Lawmakers, accountable to voters, would remain free to refine the boundaries of lawful speech through democratic processes. The public would know exactly what the rules are and could challenge them in court or at the ballot box.

This arrangement respects both free expression and the rule of law, while eliminating the opaque intermediate layer where private companies silently invent new speech restrictions beyond those democratically agreed upon.

7. Users can moderate their own experience without silencing others

One of the strongest arguments offered for platform moderation is user well‑being: people do not want their feeds flooded with content they find offensive, disturbing, or irrelevant. But protecting users from unwanted exposure does not require suppressing speech at the platform level.

Instead, platforms can empower individuals and communities to curate their own experience:

  • Robust blocking and muting tools so users can easily avoid people and content they dislike.
  • User‑controlled filters and feeds that let individuals exclude certain keywords, topics, or media types.
  • Opt‑in community norms: groups, forums, or sub‑communities could adopt their own rules, as long as the content itself remains accessible somewhere on the platform.
  • Transparent algorithms that users can adjust or override, including options to see unfiltered chronological content.

This model respects both the speaker and the listener. It recognizes that each person has different thresholds for what they find acceptable, and it allows them to tailor their experience accordingly. Instead of a centralized authority deciding what everyone is allowed to see, each user becomes the editor of their own digital environment.

Legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech does not forbid them from offering tools that help users filter what they personally see. It merely prevents them from declaring entire categories of lawful expression off‑limits to everyone.

8. A legal mandate levels the playing field and fosters healthier competition

Currently, platforms compete not just on features, but on their moderation regimes. Some promise “safe spaces,” others advertise looser policies, but all operate under constant pressure—from activists, advertisers, and governments—to demonstrate that they are “responsibly” managing speech. This leads to:

  • Constant policy churn and uncertainty
  • Performative crackdowns during media storms
  • “Safety theater” that punishes marginal users more than powerful ones

A clear legal requirement to host all lawful speech would:

  • Level the playing field: every major platform would operate under the same basic obligations.
  • Shift competition to product quality, usability, and innovation rather than speech policing.
  • Reduce external pressure and lobbying wars over moderation, since platforms could legitimately say, “We follow the law; we do not censor lawful speech.”

Smaller platforms would particularly benefit. Currently, many cannot afford large moderation teams or sophisticated AI filters and thus face disproportionate legal and reputational risks. Under a uniform lawful‑speech standard, their obligations would be simpler and clearer.

9. Principles are tested at the margins, not the center

It is easy to proclaim support for free expression when dealing with popular or widely accepted ideas. The true test comes at the margins: speech that is offensive, unpopular, or deeply wrong in the eyes of many.

History offers countless examples where the speech most worth protecting was speech many people wanted to suppress:

  • Advocates of religious freedom in societies dominated by a single faith
  • Abolitionists in pro‑slavery societies
  • Early critics of wars, interventions, or government abuses
  • Minority groups challenging entrenched social norms

In each case, dominant institutions—including private media companies—often aligned with prevailing sentiment and against those dissenting voices. Social media platforms today play a similar role as gatekeepers. When we empower them to silence what is currently despised, we create tools that future majorities can use against tomorrow’s necessary dissenters.

A rigorous commitment to hosting all lawful speech is a commitment to defending not just the speech we like, but also the speech we detest. That may be uncomfortable, but it is precisely at these uncomfortable edges that freedom either stands or collapses.

10. Conclusion: Choose law over private rule, freedom over paternalism

The internet has become the central nervous system of modern civilization. It is where we deliberate, organize, argue, learn, and imagine alternatives. In such a world, the rules governing online speech are not a minor technical or corporate matter; they are core constitutional questions, even if not always recognized as such.

Allowing social media and tech platforms to decide which lawful ideas may be expressed, and which must be suppressed, amounts to outsourcing fundamental civic decisions to entities that are:

  • Not elected
  • Not transparently accountable
  • Not bound by the same procedural safeguards as courts and legislatures

Abolishing platform content moderation and legally requiring the hosting of all lawful speech would:

  • Reassert the primacy of democratically defined law over corporate terms of service
  • Disperse the power to shape public discourse away from a handful of private actors
  • Reduce politicized, inconsistent, and opaque enforcement that corrodes trust
  • Empower individuals and communities to curate their own experience, instead of having it curated for them

Freedom of expression is not tidy. It guarantees we will encounter ideas that offend, disturb, or anger us. But the alternative—a sanitized public sphere managed by a small cadre of corporate gatekeepers—is far more dangerous. A society worthy of calling itself free should trust its citizens with the full spectrum of lawful speech and reserve the power to restrict expression to transparent, democratically accountable legal processes.

If speech is legal, it should be allowed online. No platform should be in the business of erasing lawful ideas from our shared digital spaces. The price of true freedom is tolerating speech we might strongly dislike. The reward is a more honest, resilient, and genuinely democratic public sphere.

In U.S. law, "common carriers" (such as telecom companies, postal services, and railroads) are entities that hold themselves out to the public to provide transportation or communication services indifferently.

  • Resisting Echo Chambers: Proponents argue that content moderation creates insular echo chambers and prevents users from encountering challenging or unconventional ideas.
  • The Remedy for Bad Speech is More Speech: By prohibiting moderation of legal content, proponents believe the public is trusted to evaluate information independently rather than relying on corporate arbiters to determine what is "true," "safe," or "harmful."

Major social media companies wield immense influence over the flow of information globally. Proponents of non-moderation laws express concern over the concentration of power in the hands of a few unelected technology executives.

Critics and opponents raise significant counter-arguments, including potential violations of the platforms' own First Amendment rights (compelled speech), the proliferation of hate speech and harassment, the risk of driving users toward extremist-only platforms, and technical challenges regarding international jurisdictions.

The Case for Abolishing Platform Content Moderation: Restoring the Promise of the Digital Public Square

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

When the architects of the internet first envisioned a globally connected communications network, they imagined something revolutionary: a space where every human being, regardless of wealth, status, or geographic location, could speak, publish, and be heard. For a brief, luminous period in the 1990s and early 2000s, that vision seemed within reach. Today, it lies in ruins. A handful of private corporations—Meta, Google, X, Apple, TikTok—now exercise more control over public discourse than any government, monarch, or religious institution in human history. They decide, through opaque algorithms and inconsistently applied "community guidelines," which ideas billions of people are permitted to encounter, share, and discuss. This is an unprecedented concentration of communicative power, and it should alarm anyone who takes seriously the principles underlying free expression.

This essay argues that lawmakers should abolish discretionary content moderation by major social media and technology platforms and legally require them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement. The argument rests on several reinforcing pillars: the philosophical foundations of free expression, the practical failures of the current moderation regime, the dangerous political economy of corporate speech control, the availability of superior alternatives, and the precedent established by common carrier and public accommodation law. While this position is not without complications—and I will address the strongest objections honestly—the weight of evidence and principle falls decisively on the side of open platforms.

I. The Philosophical Foundations: Why Free Expression Matters

A. The Millian Argument from Truth

John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859) remains the most powerful philosophical defense of unrestricted expression. Mill argued that silencing any opinion inflicts a harm on the human race, because if the opinion is correct, society is deprived of the opportunity to exchange error for truth; if it is wrong, society loses "the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error." This argument does not weaken in the digital age—it strengthens. The internet is the most powerful truth-discovery engine ever created, but only when it operates freely. Every suppressed claim, however objectionable, represents a lost opportunity either to correct a genuine error in mainstream thinking or to sharpen and fortify correct beliefs through challenge.

Consider the trajectory of several claims that major platforms suppressed or penalized between 2020 and 2023: the hypothesis that COVID-19 originated in a laboratory leak, skepticism about the durability of vaccine-induced immunity, questions about the efficacy of cloth masks, and concerns about myocarditis risks in young males receiving mRNA vaccines. Each of these positions was, at various points, labeled "misinformation" by platform moderators, fact-checkers, or algorithmic systems. Each was subsequently acknowledged by mainstream scientific institutions as plausible, partially correct, or entirely correct. The people who raised these points early were not rewarded for their prescience; they were silenced, demonetized, or banned. The cost was not merely personal—it was epistemic. Society's ability to respond to a pandemic was degraded because platforms arrogated to themselves the authority to determine which scientific hypotheses were permissible.

Mill anticipated precisely this danger: "The peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it."

B. The Argument from Democratic Self-Governance

Alexander Meiklejohn, the great twentieth-century theorist of the First Amendment, argued that free expression is not primarily an individual right but a structural requirement of democracy. Self-governing citizens must have access to all relevant information and arguments to make informed decisions about public policy. When platforms remove political speech, suppress news stories, or algorithmically downrank disfavored viewpoints, they do not merely inconvenience individual speakers—they corrupt the informational environment upon which democratic decision-making depends.

The suppression of the New York Post's Hunter Biden laptop story in October 2020—weeks before a presidential election—is a case study in democratic harm. Twitter locked the Post's account. Facebook reduced distribution. The story was labeled "disinformation" by dozens of former intelligence officials whose letter was amplified by legacy media. Two years later, the laptop's authenticity was confirmed by the New York Times, Washington Post, and the Department of Justice. Regardless of one's political affiliations, the implications are staggering: platform moderation decisions may have materially influenced the informational environment surrounding a presidential election. No private company should possess that power.

C. The Argument from Individual Autonomy and Dignity

Free expression is also grounded in respect for individual autonomy. To tell a person that they may not share their sincerely held beliefs—political, religious, scientific, or cultural—is to treat them as something less than a full moral agent. Content moderation, by definition, involves one party (the platform) substituting its judgment for that of both the speaker and the listener. It tells the speaker: "Your thoughts are too dangerous to be heard." It tells the listener: "You are too foolish or fragile to evaluate these ideas yourself." Both messages are deeply paternalistic and fundamentally incompatible with the liberal conception of human dignity.

II. The Practical Failures of Content Moderation

A. The Impossibility of Consistent Enforcement at Scale

Major platforms process billions of pieces of content daily. Meta alone reports moderating over 100 billion posts, comments, and messages annually. The notion that this volume of speech can be fairly and consistently adjudicated is a fantasy. Studies have repeatedly demonstrated that content moderation is riddled with errors, inconsistencies, and biases:

  • Algorithmic failures: Automated systems routinely misidentify satire, irony, counter-speech, news reporting, and academic discussion as violations. ProPublica, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and numerous academic researchers have documented how AI moderation systems disproportionately flag content in African American Vernacular English, Arabic, and other non-standard linguistic registers.

  • Human moderator inconsistency: Facebook's own internal research, revealed by whistleblower Frances Haugen, showed that human moderators agreed with each other on whether a given post violated policy only about 70% of the time—for the clearest cases. For borderline content, agreement rates were far lower. This means that whether your speech survives depends substantially on which moderator happens to review it.

  • Disproportionate impact on marginalized voices: Despite the stated goal of protecting vulnerable communities, moderation systems systematically harm them. Palestinian journalists, Black activists, LGBTQ+ advocates, sex workers, disability rights campaigners, and indigenous groups have all documented waves of unjustified content removal. During the 2021 Israel-Gaza conflict, Instagram and Facebook suppressed Palestinian voices so aggressively that even Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International issued formal condemnations. The people who most need the amplifying power of social media are frequently the first to lose it.

  • The appeals black hole: When content is wrongly removed, the appeals process is typically opaque, slow, and inadequate. Users receive form responses. They cannot confront their accusers. They have no right to a hearing. The procedural protections that liberal societies have spent centuries developing for even minor legal disputes are entirely absent.

The conclusion is inescapable: content moderation at scale does not work. It cannot work. The volume is too great, the judgments too subjective, and the stakes too high for any system—human, algorithmic, or hybrid—to operate with acceptable accuracy and fairness.

B. The Ratchet Effect

Content moderation expands inexorably. What begins as the removal of illegal content (child exploitation material, terrorist recruitment) quickly extends to "harmful" content, then to "misleading" content, then to content that violates ever-expanding and ever-more-subjective "community standards." Today, major platforms moderate for "misinformation," "hate speech," "coordinated inauthentic behavior," "dangerous organizations," "harmful health claims," and dozens of other categories, each defined by the platform itself, each subject to change without notice, and each enforced with minimal accountability.

This ratchet effect is not accidental—it is structural. Once a platform accepts the principle that it should moderate legal speech, every activist group, government official, and advertiser has an incentive to lobby for the expansion of moderation to cover their particular concern. The result is a steadily contracting sphere of permissible expression, driven not by any coherent principle but by the shifting pressures of political mobilization and commercial interest.

III. The Dangerous Political Economy of Corporate Speech Control

A. Platforms as Instruments of State Censorship

One of the most alarming developments of the past decade has been the emergence of what legal scholars have called "censorship by proxy" or "jawboning"—the practice of government officials pressuring private platforms to remove speech that the government itself would be constitutionally prohibited from suppressing.

The Missouri v. Biden litigation (now Murthy v. Missouri) revealed extensive communications between White House officials, FBI agents, CDC officials, and the Surgeon General's office on one side, and executives at Facebook, Twitter, Google, and other platforms on the other. Government officials identified specific posts and accounts they wanted suppressed. They warned of regulatory consequences for non-compliance. They held regular meetings to coordinate moderation priorities. In some cases, platforms reversed their own moderation decisions at the government's request.

This is not a hypothetical concern or a conspiracy theory—it is documented in thousands of pages of discovery materials and was found sufficiently troubling for a federal district court and the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to issue injunctions (though the Supreme Court later vacated on standing grounds without reaching the merits). The existence of discretionary content moderation creates a permanent structural vulnerability: as long as platforms can remove lawful speech, governments will pressure them to do so. Eliminating discretionary moderation eliminates the attack surface.

B. The Problem of Monopoly Power

The argument that "platforms are private companies and can set their own rules" might be compelling if the market for digital communication were competitive. It is not. Network effects, data advantages, and massive capital requirements create natural monopolies or tight oligopolies in every major category of online communication: search (Google, ~90% market share), social networking (Meta), video (YouTube), professional networking (LinkedIn), mobile app distribution (Apple and Google duopoly). When a person is banned from these platforms, they are not merely excluded from one business's premises—they are substantially excluded from public life.

The "build your own platform" response has been empirically refuted. When Parler attempted to serve as an alternative after waves of bans from mainstream platforms, Amazon Web Services terminated its hosting, Apple and Google removed its app, and its domain registrar threatened cancellation. The entire infrastructure stack has adopted content moderation norms, creating a system in which dissenting platforms can be denied the basic technical services needed to exist. This is not a free market—it is a cartel operating a permission-based speech regime.

C. The Advertiser-Driven Bias Toward Blandness

Platform content moderation is not primarily motivated by concern for user safety—it is motivated by advertiser preferences. Brands do not want their advertisements displayed alongside controversial content. This creates a systematic bias toward removing edgy, provocative, or challenging speech—precisely the speech that free expression principles are most concerned with protecting. The result is a digital public square optimized not for democratic discourse but for the commercial interests of consumer brands. Important but uncomfortable discussions about race, sexuality, religion, war, and inequality are suppressed not because they violate any coherent ethical principle but because they make advertisers nervous.

IV. The Legal Framework: Common Carriers and Public Accommodations

A. Historical Precedent

The proposal to require platforms to carry all lawful speech is not radical—it is historically grounded. American law has long recognized that certain businesses, by virtue of their monopoly power and public importance, must serve all comers without discrimination:

  • Common carriers: Telegraph companies, telephone companies, and railroads were required to transmit all messages and carry all passengers without editorial discretion. When Western Union attempted to discriminate among messages based on content, Congress and the courts put a stop to it. The principle was simple: when you operate the essential infrastructure of communication, you do not get to choose which communications to carry.

  • Public accommodations: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 required hotels, restaurants, and theaters to serve all customers regardless of race. The principle extends naturally: businesses that hold themselves open to the general public and occupy a position of market dominance must not discriminate.

Social media platforms are the telegraph companies and public accommodations of the twenty-first century. They have held themselves open to all users. They dominate the infrastructure of public discourse. They should be subject to the same non-discrimination obligations.

B. Section 230 Reform

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act currently provides platforms with immunity from liability for user-generated content while simultaneously granting them broad discretion to moderate "in good faith." This framework creates a perverse incentive structure: platforms receive the liability protections of a neutral conduit while exercising the editorial control of a publisher. Reform should condition Section 230 immunity on genuine neutrality—platforms that choose to host all lawful speech retain immunity; platforms that exercise editorial discretion accept publisher liability. This aligns incentives correctly and restores coherence to the legal framework.

C. The Texas and Florida Models

Texas (HB 20) and Florida (SB 7072) have both enacted legislation restricting the ability of large platforms to engage in content-based moderation. While these laws face ongoing constitutional challenges, they represent a serious legislative effort to address the problem. The Supreme Court's decision in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) did not categorically strike down these laws, instead remanding for further analysis. The constitutional path is narrower than critics allege, and the policy case is strong.

V. Superior Alternatives to Platform-Level Censorship

Abolishing platform-level content moderation does not mean abandoning users to a fire hose of unwanted content. Several superior alternatives exist:

A. User-Side Filtering Tools

Rather than platforms deciding what all users may see, individual users should be empowered with robust filtering tools. Want to avoid profanity? Political content? Discussions of specific topics? Users should be able to configure their own filters, subscribe to curated filter lists maintained by trusted third parties (churches, civil liberties organizations, parenting groups, academic institutions), and adjust their experience to their own preferences. This approach respects both the speaker's right to speak and the listener's right to choose—the defining feature of a liberal communications regime.

B. The Bluesky Model: Composable Moderation

The Bluesky social network has pioneered a model of "composable moderation" in which the underlying protocol carries all lawful speech, but users and communities can apply moderation "layers" of their choosing. This separates the infrastructure layer (which should be neutral) from the experience layer (which should be customizable). It is the most promising architectural approach to the moderation dilemma, and it should be the model for regulatory policy.

C. Existing Legal Remedies

Genuinely harmful speech—true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, fraud, harassment, child exploitation material—is already illegal. The appropriate response to illegal speech is law enforcement, not corporate content moderation. Platforms should be required to comply with valid legal process and remove content that courts have determined to be unlawful. They should not be permitted to go further and suppress speech that is merely unpopular, controversial, or disliked by moderators, executives, or government officials.

VI. Addressing Objections

A. "But What About Hate Speech?"

The United States, unlike many other nations, does not recognize "hate speech" as a legal category, and for good reason. The concept is irreducibly subjective. One person's "hate speech" is another's sincere religious conviction, political critique, or uncomfortable truth. History demonstrates that hate speech laws and policies are invariably weaponized against the marginalized groups they purport to protect. In the Jim Crow South, civil rights advocacy was considered dangerous and hateful speech. Today, criticism of governments in Turkey, India, Thailand, and dozens of other countries is classified as "hate speech" or "dangerous misinformation" to justify censorship.

The ACLU recognized for decades that the solution to hateful speech is more speech—counter-speech, education, social sanction—not suppression. This principle is correct, and it applies with equal force to platforms.

B. "Platforms Will Become Cesspools"

This objection underestimates both the resilience of online communities and the power of user-side tools. Early internet forums, Usenet groups, and mailing lists operated for years without centralized content moderation and produced vibrant, valuable communities. The key is shifting moderation power from the platform level to the community and individual level. Users who want a heavily curated experience can have one. Users who prefer an open information environment can have that instead. The current system denies everyone the choice by imposing a single, corporate-determined standard on billions of people.

Moreover, the "cesspool" argument proves too much. Taken seriously, it implies that the general public cannot be trusted with open communication—a premise that is incompatible with democracy itself.

C. "Private Companies Have First Amendment Rights Too"

This objection conflates two distinct issues. Individual businesses certainly have expressive rights. But when a company operates essential public communications infrastructure with monopoly power, serves billions of users, and benefits from legal immunities specifically designed to promote open discourse, the analogy to a private business choosing what to display in its shop window breaks down completely. We do not permit telephone companies to disconnect callers whose conversations they find offensive. We do not permit electric utilities to cut power to households that subscribe to disfavored publications. The principle of non-discrimination in essential services is well-established, and it should apply to the dominant communications platforms of our era.

D. "Foreign Propaganda and Bot Networks Will Flourish"

This is a legitimate concern, but it is better addressed through transparency requirements (mandatory disclosure of bot accounts, foreign state-affiliated media labeling, and provenance tracking) than through content removal. Removing content drives it underground, where it festers without rebuttal. Transparent labeling allows users to evaluate the source and credibility of information—a far more effective and democratic approach.

VII. The International Dimension

The United States has a unique opportunity—and responsibility—to model a free-expression approach to platform governance. Around the world, governments are exploiting the content moderation framework to impose increasingly authoritarian speech controls. The European Union's Digital Services Act, the UK's Online Safety Act, India's IT Rules, and Turkey's social media law all require platforms to remove broad categories of legal-but-disfavored speech. Authoritarian governments from China to Russia to Saudi Arabia use platform moderation tools and norms to suppress dissent.

If the United States requires platforms to host all lawful speech within its jurisdiction, it creates a powerful counter-model. American platforms would become genuine bastions of open expression—digital embassies of the First Amendment. Dissidents worldwide would have access to at least one legal jurisdiction where their speech is protected from both government and corporate censorship.

VIII. The Moral Urgency

We are at an inflection point. The decisions made in the next few years about platform governance will shape the communications environment for generations. The trend lines are alarming: moderation systems are becoming more aggressive, more opaque, and more responsive to government pressure. Artificial intelligence is enabling automated censorship at a scale that would have been unimaginable a decade ago. The Overton window of permissible online expression is contracting rapidly.

If we do not act, we will bequeath to our children a digital world in which a small number of corporations and governments determine which ideas may circulate and which must be suppressed. This is not the internet that was promised. It is not the information environment that a free society requires. And it is not a future that anyone who values human liberty should accept.

Conclusion

The case for abolishing platform content moderation and requiring the carriage of all lawful speech rests on converging arguments from philosophy, practical experience, political economy, legal history, and democratic theory. Free expression is not a luxury to be enjoyed only when speech is popular and comfortable—it is a foundational principle that matters most precisely when speech is controversial, offensive, or disruptive. The current content moderation regime fails by every metric: it is inaccurate, inconsistent, biased, opaque, unaccountable, vulnerable to government manipulation, and hostile to the very communities it claims to protect.

The alternative is not chaos—it is a communications infrastructure that treats lawful speech as a right rather than a privilege, that empowers individuals rather than corporations to make choices about what they see and hear, and that preserves the internet's original promise as a space of genuine intellectual freedom. We have the philosophical principles, the legal precedents, the technological tools, and the democratic mandate to build that alternative. What we need now is the political will.

The internet was born free. It is time to make it so again.
